modern_osis:
Ezra — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)

This book records the fulfillment of Jeremiah's prophecy concerning the return of the Jews from Babylon.

Its history especially teaches that every good work will meet opposition from enemies and may be damaged by the wrongdoing of friends.

Yet God will make his cause prevail, despite all obstacles and adversaries.

The restoration of the Jewish people was an event of extraordinary importance.

It helped preserve true religion in the world and prepared the way for the coming of the great Deliverer, Jesus Christ our Lord.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe proclamation of Cyrus for the rebuilding of the temple.1–4The people provide for their return.5–11
Cyrus announces the return (verses 1–4)

The Lord stirred the spirit of Cyrus.

The hearts of kings are in God's hands.

God governs the world by influencing human hearts, and whenever people do good, he is the One who moves them to do it.

During the Jewish people's captivity, God used them especially to draw the nations' attention toward himself.

Cyrus expected that those Jews who were able would willingly contribute offerings toward God's temple.

He also directed that they receive material support from his kingdom.

Those who say they wish the temple well should also act for its good.

The people prepare to return (verses 5–11)

The same God who moved Cyrus to proclaim freedom moved the captives to take advantage of that freedom.

Some were tempted to stay in Babylon.

Others had the courage to return, because the Lord stirred their hearts by his Spirit and grace.

Whatever good we do comes through God's grace.

By nature, our affections tend downward toward earthly things.

When they rise toward what is good, God is the One who raises them.

The gospel's invitations resemble Cyrus's proclamation.

Those enslaved by sin may be set free through Jesus Christ.

Anyone willing to return to God through repentance and faith finds that Christ has opened the way out of bondage into the glorious freedom of God's children.

Many who hear the good news still choose to stay in Babylon, loving their sins and refusing the risks of a holy life.

But others overcome obstacles and are willing to follow, because God has lifted their spirits above the world and sinful desires.

Thus the heavenly Canaan will be populated even though many perish in their Babylon.

The gospel's invitation will not be made in vain.

The return from exile therefore represents the redemption of sinners through Jesus Christ.
classic_reading:
[Ezra.1.1-Ezra.1.4]
Ezra
The history of this book is the accomplishment of Jeremiah's prophecy concerning the return of the Jews out of Babylon. From its contents we especially learn, that every good work will meet with opposition from enemies, and be hurt by the misconduct of friends; but that God will make his cause to prevail, notwithstanding all obstacles and adversaries. The restoration of the Jews was an event of the highest consequence, tending to preserve religion in the world, and preparing the way for the appearance of the Great Deliverer, the Lord Jesus Christ.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The proclamation of Cyrus for the rebuilding of the temple. | (1-4) |
The people provide for their return. | (5-11) |
Verses 1-4
The Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus. The hearts of kings are in the hand of the Lord. God governs the world by his influence on the spirits of men; whatever good they do, God stirs up their spirits to do it. It was during the captivity of the Jews, that God principally employed them as the means of calling the attention of the heathen to him. Cyrus took it for granted, that those among the Jews who were able, would offer free-will offerings for the house of God. He would also have them supplied out of his kingdom. Well-wishers to the temple should be well-doers for it.
[Ezra.1.5-Ezra.1.11]
Verses 5-11
The same God that raised up the spirit of Cyrus to proclaim liberty to the Jews, raised up their spirits to take the benefit. The temptation was to some to stay in Babylon; but some feared not to return, and they were those whose spirits God raised, by his Spirit and grace. Whatever good we do, is owing to the grace of God. Our spirits naturally bow down to this earth and the things of it; if they move upward in any good affections or good actions, it is God who raises them. The calls and offers of the gospel are like the proclamation of Cyrus. Those bound under the power of sin, may be made free by Jesus Christ. Whosoever will, by repentance and faith, return to God, Jesus Christ has opened the way for him, and raises him out of the slavery of sin into the glorious liberty of the children of God. Many that hear this joyful sound, choose to sit still in Babylon, are in love with their sins, and will not venture upon a holy life; but some break through all discouragements, whatever it cost them; they are those whose spirit God has raised above the world and the flesh, whom he has made willing. Thus will the heavenly Canaan be filled, though many perish in Babylon; and the gospel offer will not have been made in vain. The bringing back the Jews from captivity, represents the redemption of sinners by Jesus Christ.

Seek first God's kingdom, favor and glory; other things will then be supplied.

Their offerings were small compared with the gifts given by the leaders in David's time.

Yet because they were proportionate to the givers' abilities, they were just as acceptable to God.

The Lord will carry his people through work undertaken according to his will, directed toward his glory and dependent on his help.

Those who hear the gospel, turn away from sin and return to the Lord will be guided and protected through the dangers of the journey.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe altar and festivals.1–7The foundations of the temple laid.8–13
The altar is restored (verses 1–7)

Israel's conduct on returning to Jerusalem teaches us to begin with God.

We should do what we can in God's worship even when we cannot do everything we wish.

They could not build a temple immediately, but they would not remain without an altar.

Fear of danger should move us toward duty, not away from it.

If enemies surround us, all the more reason to seek God's friendship and continue in fellowship with him.

Our fears should drive us to our knees.

For a poor community, the prescribed sacrifices were costly.

Nevertheless, many people gave additional voluntary offerings.

They also began preparing for the temple without delay.

Whatever God calls us to do, we may trust his Providence to supply the means required.

The temple foundation is laid (verses 8–13)

As the foundation was laid, the people experienced remarkably different emotions.

Those who had known only life without a temple shouted with joy.

To them, even the foundation appeared magnificent.

We should give thanks when mercy begins, even before its work is complete.

But people who remembered the glory of the former temple wept loudly because this new building seemed likely to be so much poorer.

They had reason to grieve, especially if they mourned the sins that brought about the loss of the first temple.

Yet it was wrong to cast gloom over everyone else's joy.

They were in danger of despising the day of small things and failing to thank God for the gifts now before them.

Do not let the memory of former troubles overwhelm your gratitude for present mercies.

Chapter 3

Verses 1-7
From the proceedings of the Jews on their arrival, let us learn to begin with God, and to do what we can in the worship of God, when we cannot do what we would. They could not at once have a temple, but they would not be without an altar. Fear of danger should stir us to our duty. Have we many enemies? Then it is good to have God our Friend, and to keep up communion with him. Our fears should drive us to our knees. The sacrifices for all these solemnities were a heavy expense for so poor a company; yet besides those expressly appointed, many brought free-will offerings to the Lord. And they made preparation for the building of the temple without delay: whatever God calls us to do, we may depend upon his providence to furnish us with the needful means.
[Ezra.3.8-Ezra.3.13]
Verses 8-13
There was a remarkable mixture of affections upon laying the foundation of the temple. Those that only knew the misery of having no temple at all, praised the Lord with shouts of joy. To them, even this foundation seemed great. We ought to be thankful for the beginnings of mercy, though it be not yet perfect. But those who remembered the glory of the first temple, and considered how far inferior this was likely to be, wept with a loud voice. There was reason for it, and if they bewailed the sin that was the cause of this melancholy change, they did well. Yet it was wrong to cast a damp upon the common joys. They despised the day of small things, and were unthankful for the good they enjoyed. Let not the remembrance of former afflictions drown the sense of present mercies.

Opposition to the rebuilding (verses 1–5)

Every sincere attempt to revive true religion provokes the opposition of Satan and those under his influence.

These adversaries were the Samaritans, who had been settled in Israel's territory (2 Kings 17).

They clearly did not intend to join in worship of the Lord according to his word.

Those who discourage a good project or weaken its workers should consider whose example they are following.

The temple work is obstructed (verses 6–24)

It is an old slander to claim that the prosperity of God's church endangers kings and rulers.

Nothing could be further from the truth.

Genuine faith teaches people to respect and obey lawful authorities.

But when divine commands and human laws directly conflict, we must obey God rather than human beings, patiently accepting the consequences.

Everyone who loves the gospel should avoid even the appearance of wrongdoing, so as not to provide needless encouragement to the church's opponents.

The world is often ready to believe any accusation against God's people while refusing to listen to their defense.

The king was misled through fraudulent reports and falsehoods.

Rulers often see and hear through other people's eyes and ears and make decisions based on descriptions of events that are inaccurate or dishonest.

But God's judgment is entirely just.

He sees everything as it really is.

It was plain that they did not mean to unite in the worship of the Lord, according to his word. Let those who discourage a good work, and weaken them that are employed in it, see whose pattern they follow. ( [Ezra.4.6-Ezra.4.24] Ezr 4:6-24)

It is an old slander, that the prosperity of the church would be hurtful to kings and princes. Nothing can be more false, for true godliness teaches us to honour and obey our sovereign. But where the command of God requires one thing and the law of the land another, we must obey God rather than man, and patiently submit to the consequences. All who love the gospel should avoid all appearance of evil, lest they should encourage the adversaries of the church. Princes see and hear with other men's eyes and ears, and judge things as represented to them, which are often done falsely. But God's judgment is just; he sees things as they are.

The leaders renew the temple work (verses 1 and 2)

Construction of the temple had been interrupted for about fifteen years.

Then God sent the people two faithful ministers to urge them to resume.

It is a sign that God intends mercy for a people when he raises up prophets to help them in the work and ways of the Lord—as guides, overseers and leaders.

The prophet Haggai shows us what mighty things God accomplishes through his word and through the Spirit working with that word.

The elders answer the opposition (verses 3–17)

When we are engaged in God's work, his eye rests upon us for good and we receive his special protection.

That should encourage us to continue even when difficulties seem overwhelming.

The Jewish elders explained to their opponents what they were doing and why.

We should learn to be ready, with gentleness and reverence, to explain the hope within us and to give truthful reasons for our acts of service.

We must first understand our own responsibilities, then state them clearly.

While living in this world, we must acknowledge that our sins provoke God's anger.

Our troubles spring from human wrongdoing, while all our comforts come from his undeserved mercy.

Even when the work seems obstructed, Jesus Christ is carrying it forward.

His people are being built together as a holy temple in the Lord, a dwelling place of God through the Spirit.

In Haggai, we see what great things God does by his word, which he magnifies above all his name, and by his Spirit working with it.

The decree allows the work to resume (verses 1–12)

When God's appointed time comes to fulfill his gracious purposes for the church, he can raise up unexpected people to assist.

Zechariah directs our attention beyond Jerusalem's temple to a greater spiritual building.

Jesus Christ continues laying stone upon stone.

Let us assist his great work.

Difficulties may delay the construction, but opposition must not discourage us.

At the appointed time the work will be completed to Christ's praise.

He will set its finishing stone in place amid shouts of “Grace! Grace to it!”

The temple is completed (verses 13–22)

The gospel church, God's spiritual temple, has been under construction for a long time.

Yet it will be finished when the whole mystical body is complete.

Every believer is also a living temple, growing in the most holy faith.

Satan and our own sinful desires oppose the work.

We may work carelessly and stop and start repeatedly.

But the One who began the good work will bring it to completion.

Then the spirits of righteous people will be made perfect.

The people of Israel were freed from the sting of their earlier suffering as their sins were taken away.

They worshiped joyfully.

Let us receive God's appointed worship gladly and serve the Lord with joy.

Ezra travels to Jerusalem (verses 1–10)

Ezra went from Babylon to Jerusalem seeking the welfare of his people.

The king favored him and granted all his requests, supplying what he needed to serve his country.

Many people accompanied him.

He enjoyed the king's favor because of God's favor.

Every person and created thing can become to us only what God makes them.

We should recognize his hand in everything that happens and thank him.

The king commissions Ezra (verses 11–26)

The generosity of pagan kings in supporting God's worship put to shame the actions of many kings of Judah.

It also rebukes wealthy professing Christians who refuse to give toward God's cause.

But the weapons of Christian ministers are not physical or military weapons.

Their means of bringing people into obedience to Christ are faithful preaching, holy living, earnest prayer and patient suffering when called to it.

Ezra thanks God (verses 27 and 28)

Ezra blessed God for two things.

First, his commission. Whenever we find good in our hearts or in others', we must acknowledge that God put it there and praise him.

He is the One who works in us both to will and to do what is good.

Second, his encouragement. God had extended mercy toward Ezra.

Ezra acted bravely, yet attributed his courage to God's hand, not to his own strength.

When he supports us, we are bold and joyful.

When he withdraws his help, we become weak as water.

Whatever good we can accomplish for God or our neighbors, all the glory belongs to him.

Ezra grieves over Israel's wrongdoing (verses 1–4)

Even the most careful leaders may fail to see some of the corruption hidden among the people.

Some Israelites had disobeyed God's explicit command concerning marriage with the nations (Deuteronomy 7).

Their unwillingness to trust God's complete sufficiency lay behind the compromises they made to help themselves.

Through those relationships they exposed themselves and their children to the idolatry that had already ruined their church and nation.

People who merely profess religion may dismiss such concerns or explain away God's commands about separation.

Those who know Scripture well recognize their seriousness.

It should astonish and grieve faithful believers when people who profess Christ defend serious wrongdoing.

Everyone claiming to be God's people should support those who stand and act against sin and irreverence.

Ezra confesses the people's sins (verses 5–15)

The sacrifice, especially the evening sacrifice, pointed toward the Lamb of God, who in the latter time would take away sin through his own offering.

Ezra confessed his people's sins in a spirit of repentance.

There is comfort for true penitents: although sins reach to heaven, God's mercy also reaches to heaven.

Ezra spoke with shame.

Genuine repentance needs holy shame as well as sorrow.

He spoke with amazement.

The more we consider guilt, the worse sin appears.

Let us cry, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner.”

Ezra also spoke with fear.

There is hardly a clearer sign of approaching ruin than returning to wrongdoing after severe judgments and great deliverances.

Everyone in God's church should be astonished that they have not exhausted the Lord's patience and brought destruction upon themselves.

What, then, of the openly ungodly?

The true penitent has nothing to plead in self-defense.

But our heavenly Advocate pleads powerfully on our behalf.

[Ezra.9.5-Ezra.9.15]
Verses 5-15
The sacrifice, especially the evening sacrifice, was a type of the blessed Lamb of God, who in the evening of the world, was to take away sin by the sacrifice of himself. Ezra's address is a penitent confession of sin, the sin of his people. But let this be the comfort of true penitents, that though their sins reach to the heavens, God's mercy is in the heavens. Ezra, speaking of sin, speaks as one much ashamed. Holy shame is as necessary in true repentance as holy sorrow. Ezra speaks as much amazed. The discoveries of guilt cause amazement; the more we think of sin, the worse it looks. Say, God be merciful to me sinner. Ezra speaks as one much afraid. There is not a surer or saddler presage of ruin, than turning to sin, after great judgments, and great deliverances. Every one in the church of God, has to wonder that he has not wearied out the Lord's patience, and brought destruction upon himself. What then must be the case of the ungodly? But though the true penitent has nothing to plead in his own behalf, the heavenly Advocate pleads most powerfully for him.

Verses 1-5
Shechaniah owned the national guilt. The case is sad, but it is not desperate; the disease threatening, but not incurable. Now that the people begin to lament, a spirit of repentance seems to be poured out; now there is hope that God will forgive, and have mercy. The sin that rightly troubles us, shall not ruin us. In melancholy times we must observe what makes for us, as well as against us. And there may be good hopes through grace, even where there is the sense of great guilt before God. The case is plain; what has been done amiss, must be undone again as far as possible; nothing less than this is true repentance. Sin must be put away, with a resolution never to have any thing more to do with it. What has been unjustly got, must be restored. Arise, be of good courage. Weeping, in this case, is good, but reforming is better. As to being unequally yoked with unbelievers, such marriages, it is certain, are sinful, and ought not to be made; but now they are not null, as they were before the gospel did away the separation between Jews and Gentiles.
[Ezra.10.6-Ezra.10.14]
Verses 6-14
There is hope concerning people, when they are convinced, not only that it is good to part with their sins, but that it is necessary; we must do it, or we are undone. So rich is the mercy, and so plenteous the redemption of God, that there is hope for the vilest who hear the gospel, and are willing to accept of free salvation. When sinners mourn for their sins, and tremble at the word of God, there is hope that they will forsake them. To affect others with godly sorrow or love to God, we must ourselves be affected. It was carefully agreed how this affair should be carried on. That which is hastily resolved on seldom proves lasting.
[Ezra.10.15-Ezra.10.44]
Verses 15-44
The best reformers can but do their endeavour; when the Redeemer himself shall come to Zion, he shall effectually turn away ungodliness from Jacob. And when sin is repented of and forsaken, God will forgive it; but the blood of Christ, our Sin-offering, is the only atonement which takes away our guilt. No seeming repentance or amendment will benefit those who reject Him, for self-dependence proves them still unhumbled. All the names written in the book of life, are those of penitent sinners, not of self-righteous persons, who think they have no need of repentance.
